• Type: moss (liverwort)
  • Origin: Asia
  • Growth rate: medium
  • Height: 3 - 5+ cm
  • Light demand: low
  • CO2: low

• Other names: Pellia moss
  • Tank size: any
  • Optimal lighting: moderate to high
  • Substrate: any
  • Growth rate: moderate to fast
  • Placement in tank: foreground and midground
  • Size: up to 20 cm or more
  • Leaf size: 2.5 to 3.5 cm
  • Fertilizers: not needed to low
  • CO2: not needed to low
  • Propagation: splitting
  • Colour: dark green

Monosolenium tenerum has a very limited subtropical Asiatic distribution. It can be found from northeast India, southern China and Taiwan to southern Japan. Even there, the species occurs in only a few isolated areas.

As a result of accidental dispersal by humans, it has also been documented in Nepal.

In the wild, Monosolenium tenerum grows emersed in high-humidity habitats. It is not a fully aquatic plant, and there are no reports of it growing submerged in the wild.

It is a semi-terrestrial liverwort that inhabits damp places, growing on moist shaded soil along forest streams and rivers.

It is a brittle plant, and pieces break off easily, so it is best to place it in the aquarium attached to stones with fishing line or in small clumps among other plants such as Eleocharis. Once Monosolenium has established itself, it is very undemanding.

Description

Monosolenium tenerum is a perennial plant that comprises a thallus, so technically it has no organised, distinct parts such as leaves and stems. It has relatively thin, dark green, fork-like branched thalli. Each thallus (the so-called 'leaves') is generally 2.5 to 3.5 cm long and 5 – 8 mm broad, with a thickened midrib and thinner semi-translucent wings with wavy margins. They are smooth on top, with no air pores or reticulations. Beneath the thalli are numerous rhizoids (hairlike organs that help anchor the plant to hardscape or decorations).

Compared with similar plants

  • Subwassertang (Lomariopsis lineata): its thallus is more transparent, thinner, darker green, more flexible and less fragile. It has no midrib and a rounder, irregular growth pattern, while Monosolenium tenerum has mostly uniform, pointed growth.
  • Riccia fluitans (Crystalwort): Monosolenium tenerum looks like a larger, darker Riccia. Crystalwort has air pores that help it float, whereas Monosolenium tenerum has none and is heavier than water, so it sinks.

Tank size

It can fit any vessel, from plastic or glass containers, jars and vases to large tanks. Under optimal conditions it can grow very fast and quickly overtake nano tanks, and it is hard to keep in one place, so it is not suited to a nicely aquascaped large planted tank. The recommended tank size is about 40 litres.

Lighting

It needs moderate to high lighting to grow optimally. Under such light it grows visibly fast and releases a great deal of oxygen. Bright light produces more compact, bushier growth. Lights should ideally be on for at least 8 hours daily. It is not the best plant for low-tech tanks: under low light it grows upward with longer gaps between thalli, and the leaves become thinner and darker.

Substrate

It does not require a substrate, as it mainly takes nutrients from the water column, so do not push it into the substrate. It can be attached to stones, rocks, driftwood, bogwood or any decoration, and will attach and grow on most surfaces.

Flow

It prefers still water. Strong water flow may make the plant drift around the tank and break off parts of it.

CO2 and fertilisation

CO2 supplementation is not necessary, but without CO2 growth in submerged conditions can be painfully slow and stringy. High-light plants must be balanced in terms of CO2, nutrients and lighting, otherwise algae will appear. It will grow without added nutrients, but regular fertiliser makes it grow faster and healthier. It responds positively to a high phosphate level (1.5 – 2 mg/l), so periodic fertilisation is recommended. If you keep shrimp with it, note that high CO2 levels and copper (present in most fertilisers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Difficulty and placement

Care is relatively easy: it is one of the few plants that can grow in extreme pH, temperature and hardness conditions. Maintenance is tricky, however, because the plant is very delicate and breaks easily, so it may spread everywhere and overstuff the tank. Its growth form depends on CO2, nutrients and light; in low-tech tanks it will be less decorative. It suits a paludarium with free excess CO2 very well. It can be used in the foreground and midground. Grown emersed in high humidity, growth is fairly fast; submersed, growth is slow to moderate.

Planting

  • Floating: simply throw it in the tank. Being heavier than water, it will find a spot it likes. Its leaves have numerous rhizoids that serve as roots and anchor the plant.
  • Attaching to rock and driftwood: tie it to driftwood or a rock with thread or fishing line. There is no need to remove the thread, as the plant will grow over it.
  • Wall, ball, etc.: use plastic mesh and suction cups to hold it against the tank wall. Fold the mesh in half, hold it with suction cups and stuff the plant inside to form a wall. The plant will grow through the mesh and cover all the spaces.

Propagation

It is propagated by division: break pieces off the plant and attach them to surfaces or hardscape. When the plant grows too thickly (thalli touching and overlapping), it is time to divide it, which also increases its growth rate.

Dry start method

Since in the wild it colonises moist soil in subtropical countries, it can also be grown with the Dry Start Method (DSM), which boosts the development of slow-growing plants, cycles the substrate and removes algae problems. It also makes the plant a great choice for paludariums.

Common problems

  • Brittle structure: easily damaged during maintenance, and fragments scatter and grow where you don't want them. Handle it extremely carefully.
  • Hard to plant: it has no well-developed root system, and under optimal conditions tiny oxygen bubbles form on the leaf tips, so unattached plants may float a bit before sinking somewhere in the tank. Attach it to something.
  • Invasiveness: every broken part starts to grow, so it can be extremely hard to get rid of. Handle it extremely carefully.
  • Leggy bottom leaves: when it gets very large, the lower portions may die back. Check the lighting, which is usually the main reason.
  • Hard to trim: it is very difficult to shape and aquascape with, and trimming is almost impossible because of its brittleness. Provide optimal conditions so the plant does not grow tall.
  • Decaying: if something gets on the plant, it may start to rot at that spot. Keep the water clean with regular maintenance.

Benefits

  • Versatility: it can grow emersed and submersed.
  • Easy to move around, especially when attached to wood or rocks.
  • Hiding place for small fish, fry and shrimp.
  • Foraging place: a buffet of biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.

Monosolenium tenerum is adaptable to a wide range of water parameters. You can even grow it in a jar on a windowsill before putting it in the tank.

  • Temperature: optimal 20 – 28 °C. Despite its subtropical origin, it can stay alive in colder water, tolerating temperatures as low as 10 °C.
  • pH: it does not care much about pH, but appreciates values between 6.0 – 8.0.
  • Hardness: very adaptable, thriving from soft to hard water at 2 – 16 GH.

Keep Monosolenium tenerum only with dwarf shrimp and small freshwater fish that are unlikely to damage it, as it is very delicate. Avoid fish that disturb the substrate near the plant (plecos or catfish) or find it too palatable, such as silver dollars, Buenos Aires tetras, koi, goldfish, oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey, clown loaches and African cichlids. Most crayfish and freshwater crabs are also a poor combination, as they cut, eat and uproot everything in the tank.

Aquarium plant from tissue culture in closed cup. The Asian Monosolenium tenerum is an attractive liverwort, 2-5 cm high, which looks most like a giant Riccia that simply stays at the bottom, where it forms cushions. This plant is mistakenly known as Pellia.

Monosolenium tenerum (previously known as Pellia endiviifolia) is a controversial plant. It is easy to grow, but its invasive nature and fragile structure require more maintenance, so place it only in tanks with suitable setups. Alternatives that look similar but stay in a clump better are Subwassertang and Crystalwort.

Land colonisation by plants started in the middle of the Ordovician period (about 470 million years ago). Thalloid liverworts, together with hornworts and mosses, are considered among the earliest diverging land plants. In 1849 the plant was described by the British botanist William Griffith; its unusual combination of characteristics led many scientists, for decades, to believe that he had largely imagined it.

Etymology: the origin of 'Monosolenium' is unclear; presumably it is made of Mono ('alone') + Solenium (from Solanum, 'nightshade'). 'Tenerum' is Latin for 'soft, delicate, or tender'.
